what_it_does: DRAM (the main memory chips that hold data while a computer is running) stores information as tiny electrical charges in cells arranged in rows and columns. A known security vulnerability called RowHammer showed that repeatedly reading from one row of memory can accidentally flip bits in the rows immediately above and below it, because the electrical noise bleeds into neighboring rows through the silicon substrate. This paper reports a newly discovered and more dangerous phenomenon called ColumnDisturb: activating a single row disturbs cells that share the same vertical wires (called bitlines or columns) across many separate sub-sections of the chip simultaneously — in some tested chips, a single row access can disturb up to 3,072 rows spread throughout the chip at once, which is vastly more destructive than classic RowHammer. The authors measured this effect on 216 DDR4 chips and 4 HBM2 chips (a high-bandwidth memory type used in GPUs) from three major manufacturers, varying temperature, data patterns, and timing settings. They also show that ColumnDisturb interacts dangerously with proposals to save power by skipping periodic memory refresh for cells that hold their charge for a long time, since ColumnDisturb can corrupt those cells before the extended refresh period expires.
